title: Like a weaned child (Psalm 130 [131])
hookLine: three verses about a quieted soul that doesn't grasp at great things

lines: A TODDLER ON A LAP: CONTENT.
cards: Watch a hungry baby for thirty seconds. Everything is wanting: crying, reaching, grabbing at the one thing that will make it better, right now. Then watch a toddler a year or two later, on a parent's lap after a long day.
Not grabbing. Not asking for anything. Just leaning back, heavy and content, because being held is enough.
Two very different ways to be a child. And a psalm only three verses long says a soul can learn the second one.

teach.b: It's another gradual psalm, headed as David's, and it starts by letting go of ambition.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, my heart is not exalted: nor are my eyes lofty. Neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me." First, who's talking.
The heading gives it to a king, somebody with every reason to grasp at great things, and he says: I've stopped. I don't need to understand everything or run everything. Second, the picture.

teach.h: NOT A NURSING BABY. A WEANED CHILD.
teach.b: The Douay follows the Latin: "As a child that is weaned is towards his mother, so reward in my soul."

teach.h: A CHILD AT REST WITH ITS MOTHER.
teach.b: The Hebrew is plainer: I have calmed and quieted my soul, like a weaned child with its mother. Weaned is the key, and the Hebrew word is gamul.
A mother in the Second Book of Maccabees reminds her son that she "gave thee suck three years." A nursing baby on its mother's lap wants one thing and cries until it gets it.

teach.h: LET ISRAEL HOPE IN THE LORD.
teach.b: A weaned child can sit on the same lap and want nothing but the closeness.

teach.h: AS A CHILD THAT IS WEANED.
teach.b: So this isn't a soul that feels nothing. It's a soul that has stopped demanding, content to be held. Third, the mother.

The psalm names only a child and its mother, but some readers hear God in the mother's place, with the psalmist resting on her lap. Saint Thérèse's little way, which we met back in the saints, breathes the same air.
Then the psalm turns to the whole people: "Let Israel hope in the Lord, from henceforth now and for ever."

how: Catholics pray Psalm 130 [131] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and some use it for quiet prayer, repeating its short verses slowly as a way of resting in God.

o: a newborn still at its mother's breast
a child crying out to be fed
weaned: a child who no longer nurses

games.q: what's inside the psalm — tap the pairs.

s: a weaned child in the psalm means a child who feels nothing
it means a child who has stopped demanding and is content to be held.
a weaned child could be three years old
a mother in Second Maccabees says she nursed her son three years: old enough to sit on a lap and want nothing.
the psalm is headed as a king's prayer
it's given to David, someone with every reason to grasp at great things.

games.q: you're a king with power to chase every great thing. the psalmist has a choice about his heart. what does he say he's done?
o: stopped walking in great matters, and quieted himself.
games.why: "Neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me." he has quieted himself like a weaned child.

practice: Settle into your chair, let it take your full weight, and let your hands open in your lap. Notice what you're reaching for, the answer, the outcome, the thing you want to happen, and for two minutes, don't reach.
If you pray, rest in God the way a child rests on a parent's lap, wanting nothing but to be there; if you don't, rest in being held up by the chair and the floor.

wordCard.voice: Gamul. Hebrew for weaned, a child who no longer nurses, content simply to be held: the psalm's picture of a quiet soul. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: weaned, a child who no longer nurses, content to rest on its mother.

carryVoice: Your line: quieted. Not empty, just done grasping at great things. Day one hundred eighty-eight.
